_readme: ONE table of cases, read by BOTH agent/tests/db-path.test.js and
api/tests/test_db_path.py. It is the only thing keeping
agent/src/utils/db-path.js and api/db_path.py in step.
They were previously 'kept in step by the tests on each side', which is
how they came to disagree about what a connection string even is: Node
keyed redaction on '://' while Python keyed it on ':/'. Node therefore
printed 'postgresql:/user:PASSWORD@host/db' verbatim -- out of the very
guard whose purpose is to protect it -- while Python mangled the real
Windows path 'C:/Users/x/data.db' into 'C://<redacted>'. Four review
rounds passed over that, because neither suite ever ran the other's
inputs.
Add a case here, not to one suite. Both sides must agree byte for byte.
cases[]  input -> expected output of redactCredentials/redact_credentials.
'verdict' is ALSO the expected verdict of
assertDatabaseTarget/assert_database_target, because the two
share one predicate and one flag therefore pins both:
'path'     an ordinary filesystem path. Accepted, and the
redacted output is the input BYTE-IDENTICAL.
'remote'   a libSQL/Turso URL the product can actually reach.
Accepted, and the redacted output keeps the scheme
and host but never userinfo, path or query -- a
Turso URL carries its token in '?authToken='.
'refused'  anything else. assert* must raise, and the
redacted output is coarsened to
'<scheme-or-redacted>://<redacted>'.
'remote' exists because the deployed product runs on
libsql://...turso.io. A guard that refuses every '<scheme>://'
refuses the URL production boots on, and a redactor that
coarsens every '://' makes the boot log stop saying which
database is live.
'forbidden' lists substrings that must NOT appear in the
redacted output or in the rejection message.
redos[]  input = unit*count + suffix; must complete within max_ms.
Non-string inputs (None/null, undefined, 5) are deliberately absent:
str(None) is 'None' but String(null) is 'null', so their coercion is
language-specific and cannot be shared. Each suite covers those locally.

cases.label: a plain absolute path
a path containing '@' — a legal filesystem character
a path containing ':' not followed by '/'
a dated backup directory, ':' mid-path
a relative path
a bare filename
a Windows drive path — one letter, one slash, no '@'
a lower-case Windows drive path
the empty string
the deployed Turso URL — accepted, and the host survives so the boot log still names the database
a Turso URL carrying userinfo — accepted, but the credential does not survive
a Turso URL carrying its token in the query — the query is dropped, not kept
a password containing '@' cannot split the authority — the LAST '@' wins
an https Turso target
a wss target with a port — the port is part of the host and survives
a ws target on localhost
an http target with a path — the path is dropped, the host is kept
an upper-case scheme — RFC 3986 schemes are case-insensitive
an allowed scheme with a SINGLE slash — no authority to trust, so fail closed
an allowed scheme naming no host at all — nothing to reach, so fail closed
an allowed scheme after a real path prefix — the prefix is not the scheme
an allowed scheme with leading whitespace — not exactly a scheme, so fail closed
an allowed scheme with a trailing character — 'libsqlx' is not 'libsql'
a Windows drive prefix in front of an allowed scheme — still not a target
a postgresql URL — the canonical case
the pathlib-collapsed single-slash form — FINDING 1, leaked verbatim on Node
no scheme at all before ':/' — FINDING 1, leaked verbatim on Node
no scheme at all before '://'
a digit-led scheme, single slash
a digit-led scheme, double slash
a punctuation-led scheme, double slash
a punctuation-led scheme, single slash
a scheme-shaped run after a real path prefix
an embedded scheme after a legitimate-looking directory prefix
a short postgresql URL
sqlite:/// — three slashes, no authority, nothing to leak
postgres://
mysql://
mongodb://
a one-character scheme with an authority — drive-shaped but '//' opens userinfo
a one-character scheme with a single slash but userinfo — the '@' rule is what catches this
a drive letter followed by '//' is an authority, not a drive
a real Windows drive prefix in front of a real connection string
a drive-shaped prefix with a SECOND ':/' later is not exempt (fail closed)
a lone '://'
a lone ':/'
a leading null byte
whitespace padding
a non-ASCII scheme-shaped prefix

4M scheme characters followed by a separator
an allowed scheme followed by a 4M-character authority
